The Kingdom of Great Britain was created earlier, in 1707.

The Irish Free State came in 1922.

questions.question: The cross of St Patrick on the Union Flag is described how?
options: A diagonal red cross on a white ground
A red cross on a white ground
A diagonal white cross on a blue ground
questions.answer: A diagonal red cross on a white ground
questions.explanation:
St Patrick (Ireland) is a diagonal red cross on a white ground.

St George (England) is an upright red cross on a white ground.

St Andrew (Scotland) is a diagonal white cross on a blue ground.

The red dragon is the Welsh flag.

questions.question: Roughly how many people lived in the British Empire at its height in the Victorian period?
questions.explanation:
The Empire had an estimated population of more than 400 million.

'About 13 million' relates to the number of British citizens who emigrated between 1853 and 1913 — relevant to emigration, not the Empire's population.

questions.question: The repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 promoted which policy?
questions.explanation:
Repealing the Corn Laws in 1846 promoted free trade by allowing cheaper grain imports.

Protectionism is the opposite.

Nationalisation relates to the post-1945 government, and devolution to powers for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

questions.question: The Crimean War (1853–56) was fought against which country?
questions.explanation:
Britain, with Turkey and France, fought against Russia in the Crimean War.

France was an ally in this war, not the enemy.

Germany and Spain were not involved.

questions.question: Queen Victoria introduced which medal during the Crimean War?
questions.explanation:
Queen Victoria introduced the Victoria Cross to honour acts of valour.

The other awards are real honours but not the one she introduced during the Crimean War.

questions.question: In the 19th century, a famine in Ireland was caused by the failure of which crop?
questions.explanation:
The Irish famine was caused by the failure of the potato crop, on which many people depended; a million died and a million and a half emigrated.

The other crops were not the cause of the famine.

questions.question: Which author, born in India, wrote The Jungle Book and the poem 'If'?
questions.explanation:
Rudyard Kipling, born in India, wrote The Jungle Book and 'If', and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907.

Dickens, Stevenson and Hardy were other notable authors but not the writer of these works.

questions.question: Whose assassination in 1914 helped trigger the First World War?
questions.explanation:
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria on 28 June 1914 triggered the chain of events leading to WWI.

The other figures were involved in 20th-century history but were not the assassinated trigger.

questions.question: In the First World War, Britain fought as part of which side?
questions.explanation:
Britain was part of the Allied Powers (with France, Russia and others).

The Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Ottoman Empire) were the enemy in WWI.

The Axis relates to WWII, and the Warsaw Pact to the Cold War.

questions.question: The 1916 uprising against British rule in Dublin was known as what?
questions.explanation:
The Easter Rising of 1916 was an uprising against the British in Dublin.

The Glorious Revolution (1688) brought William of Orange to the throne.

The Jacobite Rising supported the exiled Stuarts.

The Peasants' Revolt was a medieval event.

questions.question: In which year did the world enter the 'Great Depression'?
questions.explanation: The Great Depression began in 1929, causing mass unemployment in parts of the UK. 1918 is the end of WWI, 1939 the start of WWII, and 1945 the end of WWII.

questions.question: When did the BBC begin the world's first regular television service?
questions.explanation:
The BBC began the world's first regular television service in 1936.

It started radio broadcasts in 1922 — so 1922 is relevant to radio. 1969 and 1990 relate to other events (voting age; the first web transfer).

questions.question: In WWII, the Axis powers were Germany, Italy and which other country?
questions.explanation:
The Axis powers were Germany, Italy and Japan.

Russia (the Soviet Union) was invaded by Germany and joined the Allies.

France and Poland were on the Allied side.

questions.question: The D-Day landings of 6 June 1944 took place where?
questions.explanation:
Allied forces landed in Normandy on D-Day (6 June 1944).

Dunkirk relates to the 1940 evacuation.

Berlin was the German capital, reached later.

Sicily saw earlier Allied action in Italy but was not the D-Day location.

questions.question: Which British scientist developed radar?
questions.explanation:
Sir Robert Watson-Watt, a Scotsman, developed radar.

John Logie Baird developed television.

Sir Frank Whittle developed the jet engine.

Sir Bernard Lovell built the Jodrell Bank radio telescope.

questions.question: Who developed the jet engine in Britain in the 1930s?
questions.explanation:
Sir Frank Whittle, an RAF engineer officer, developed the jet engine.

Sir Christopher Cockerell invented the hovercraft.

James Goodfellow invented the cash-dispensing ATM.

Sir Peter Mansfield co-invented the MRI scanner.

questions.question: Who invented the hovercraft in the 1950s?
questions.explanation:
Sir Christopher Cockerell invented the hovercraft.

Sir Frank Whittle developed the jet engine.

Alan Turing devised the Turing machine.

John MacLeod co-discovered insulin.

questions.question: The first cash-dispensing ATM was put into use by Barclays Bank in 1967 in which London area?
questions.explanation:
The first ATM, invented by James Goodfellow, was installed by Barclays in Enfield, north London, in 1967.

Greenwich, Canterbury and Stratford are associated with other landmarks and events.

questions.question: The world's first 'test-tube baby' (from IVF) was born in 1978 in which town?
questions.explanation:
IVF was pioneered by Sir Robert Edwards and Patrick Steptoe, and the first test-tube baby was born in Oldham, Lancashire, in 1978.

The other places are associated with other scientific work.

questions.question: Dolly the sheep, the first cloned mammal, was created in which year?
questions.explanation: Dolly the sheep was cloned in 1996 by a team led by Sir Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell. 1953 relates to the discovery of DNA's structure, 1978 to the first IVF baby, and 1990 to the first web transfer.

questions.question: In 1947, independence was granted to nine countries, including which of these?
questions.explanation:
In 1947, independence was granted to nine countries, including India, Pakistan and Ceylon (now Sri Lanka).

Other African and Caribbean colonies gained independence over the following 20 years, so Kenya and Nigeria came later.

questions.question: Which Prime Minister gave the famous 'wind of change' speech about decolonisation?
questions.explanation:
Harold Macmillan, PM in the late 1950s, gave the 'wind of change' speech.

Clement Attlee led the 1945 government, Churchill led Britain in WWII, and Thatcher became PM in 1979.

questions.question: The Education Act 1944 ('the Butler Act') introduced what in England and Wales?
questions.explanation:
The Butler Act (1944) introduced free secondary education and the primary/secondary division.

The NHS was created in 1948 under a different reform.

The other options are not what the Act introduced.

questions.question: In 1948, people from where were invited to come and work in Britain?
questions.explanation:
In 1948, people from the West Indies were invited to come and help rebuild Britain.

Later, workers were also recruited from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh.

The other regions were not part of this post-war recruitment.

questions.question: Which two famous pop groups were prominent in the 'Swinging Sixties'?
options: The Beatles and The Rolling Stones
questions.answer: The Beatles and The Rolling Stones
questions.explanation:
The Beatles and The Rolling Stones were prominent in the 1960s and continue to influence music.

The other bands are real British acts but are not the two named in the handbook for the 'Swinging Sixties'.

questions.question: In which year did the UK join the European Economic Community (EEC)?
questions.explanation: The UK joined the EEC in 1973. 1957 is when the EEC was founded by the Treaty of Rome. 2020 is when the UK left the EU (Brexit). 1999 relates to devolution.

questions.question: Margaret Thatcher trained in which two professions before entering politics?
questions.explanation:
Margaret Thatcher, the grocer's daughter from Grantham, trained as a chemist and a lawyer.

The other professions are distractors and do not match the handbook.

questions.question: The Conservative government from 2015 to 2024 included several Prime Ministers. Which of these was one of them?
questions.explanation:
Conservative PMs in that period included David Cameron, Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak.

Tony Blair and Gordon Brown were earlier Labour PMs, and Keir Starmer became Labour PM in 2024.

questions.question: Who was the organist at Westminster Abbey and developed a distinctly British musical style?
questions.explanation:
Henry Purcell was the organist at Westminster Abbey and developed a distinct British style.

Handel was German-born and wrote Messiah.

Holst wrote The Planets, and Elgar the Pomp and Circumstance Marches.

questions.question: Gilbert and Sullivan are famous for writing which kind of work?
questions.explanation:
Gilbert and Sullivan wrote comic operas such as HMS Pinafore, The Pirates of Penzance and The Mikado.

Detective novels relate to Agatha Christie and Conan Doyle.

War poetry relates to Wilfred Owen and Siegfried Sassoon.

questions.question: Which composer's works include Peter Grimes and Billy Budd, and who founded the Aldeburgh festival?
questions.explanation:
Benjamin Britten wrote Peter Grimes and Billy Budd and founded the Aldeburgh festival.

Walton wrote Façade; Vaughan Williams was influenced by folk music; Purcell was a much earlier composer.

questions.question: The Edinburgh Festival Fringe is best known for showcasing what?
questions.explanation:
The Edinburgh Festival Fringe showcases mainly theatre and comedy, often experimental.

Classical painting relates to galleries and the Turner Prize.

Motor racing and horse racing are sports, not the Fringe.

questions.question: Which landscape painter is most famous for works of Dedham Vale?
questions.explanation:
John Constable is famous for painting Dedham Vale on the Suffolk–Essex border.

Thomas Gainsborough painted portraits in country settings.

Henry Moore was a sculptor.

David Hockney is associated with pop art.

questions.question: Which architect designed the Queen's House at Greenwich and the Banqueting House in Whitehall?
questions.explanation:
Inigo Jones designed the Queen's House at Greenwich and the Banqueting House.

Sir Christopher Wren designed St Paul's Cathedral.

Robert Adam is relevant to the Royal Crescent in Bath.

Sir Edwin Lutyens designed the Cenotaph.

questions.question: Which 18th-century figure designed landscapes so they appeared natural, and often said a place had 'capabilities'?
questions.explanation:
Lancelot 'Capability' Brown designed natural-looking landscapes around country houses.

Gertrude Jekyll designed colourful gardens, often with Lutyens.

Robert Adam was an architect, and Sir Norman Foster is a modern architect.

questions.question: Which British author wrote Oliver Twist and Great Expectations?
questions.explanation:
Charles Dickens wrote Oliver Twist and Great Expectations, and created characters such as Scrooge and Mr Micawber.

Jane Austen wrote Pride and Prejudice.

Thomas Hardy wrote Far from the Madding Crowd.

Graham Greene wrote Brighton Rock.

questions.question: Which poet wrote Paradise Lost?
questions.explanation:
John Milton wrote Paradise Lost.

William Wordsworth wrote 'The Daffodils'.

William Blake wrote 'The Tyger'.

Lord Byron wrote 'She Walks in Beauty'.

questions.question: What is the day after Christmas Day called?
questions.explanation:
Boxing Day (26 December) is the day after Christmas and a public holiday.

New Year's Day is 1 January.

Shrove Tuesday is the day before Lent.

The other option is a distractor.

questions.question: The Jewish festival remembered by lighting candles on a menorah over eight days is called what?
questions.explanation:
Hanukkah is a Jewish festival lasting eight days, marked by lighting a menorah.

Diwali is a Hindu and Sikh festival.

Vaisakhi is a Sikh festival.

Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan for Muslims.

questions.question: Vaisakhi, celebrated on 14 April, is a festival for which faith?
questions.explanation:
Vaisakhi is a Sikh festival celebrating the founding of the Khalsa, on 14 April.

Diwali is celebrated by Hindus and Sikhs.

Eid festivals are Muslim, and Hanukkah is Jewish.

questions.question: Mothering Sunday falls when?
options: On the third Sunday in June
questions.explanation:
Mothering Sunday (Mother's Day) is the Sunday three weeks before Easter.

The third Sunday in June is Father's Day. 14 February is Valentine's Day, and 1 April is April Fool's Day.

questions.question: Rented land where people grow fruit and vegetables is called what?
questions.explanation:
An allotment is rented land for growing fruit and vegetables.

A croft was a small Scottish farm, relevant to the Highland Clearances.

A plantation relates to settlement in Ulster.

A 'common' is a different kind of shared land.

questions.question: The satirical magazine first published in the 1840s was called what?
questions.explanation:
Punch was first published in the 1840s and was the most famous satirical magazine.

Private Eye continues the tradition of satire today.

Hansard is the official record of parliamentary proceedings, not a satirical magazine.

questions.question: In which year was the National Trust founded?
questions.explanation: The National Trust was founded in 1895 by three volunteers. 1984 relates to the establishment of the Turner Prize. 1945 and 1707 relate to other events (post-war government; Act of Union).

questions.question: The clock tower housing Big Ben was renamed in 2012 in honour of the Queen. What is it now called?
questions.explanation:
The tower was named Elizabeth Tower in honour of Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee in 2012.

Big Ben is actually the nickname of the great bell.

The Shard is a separate modern skyscraper.

questions.question: The spiritual leader of the Church of England is who?
questions.explanation:
The Archbishop of Canterbury is the spiritual leader of the Church of England.

The monarch is its head.

The Moderator chairs the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland.

The Pope leads the Roman Catholic Church.

questions.question: Which flower is associated with Northern Ireland?
questions.explanation:
The shamrock is associated with Northern Ireland.

The daffodil is associated with Wales, the rose with England, and the thistle with Scotland.

questions.question: The Paralympic Games have their origins in the work of Dr Ludwig Guttman at which hospital?
questions.explanation:
Dr Ludwig Guttman's work at Stoke Mandeville hospital in Buckinghamshire led to the Paralympics.

St Thomas' is relevant to Florence Nightingale's nursing school.

The other hospitals are distractors here.

questions.question: Sir Steve Redgrave won gold medals in which sport across five consecutive Olympic Games?
questions.explanation:
Sir Steve Redgrave won rowing golds in five consecutive Olympics.

Cycling relates to Sir Chris Hoy and Sir Bradley Wiggins.

Athletics relates to figures like Mo Farah, and sailing to Dame Ellen MacArthur.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?
questions.explanation:
Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland.

Cardiff is the capital of Wales, Edinburgh of Scotland.

Dublin is the capital of the Republic of Ireland, which is a separate country and not part of the UK.

questions.question: What is the National Anthem of the UK?
questions.explanation:
The National Anthem is 'God Save the King (or Queen)'.

'Land of Hope and Glory' is played at the Last Night of the Proms.

'Rule Britannia' and 'Jerusalem' are patriotic songs but not the national anthem.

questions.question: Which court in Scotland hears the most serious cases, such as murder?
questions.explanation:
In Scotland the most serious cases, such as murder, are heard at the High Court with a judge and jury.

The Sheriff Court hears less serious cases.

Magistrates' Courts and County Courts operate in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, not Scotland.

questions.question: Sir Jackie Stewart is a Scottish former champion in which sport?
questions.explanation:
Sir Jackie Stewart won the Formula 1 world championship three times.

Cycling relates to Sir Chris Hoy, rowing to Sir Steve Redgrave, and athletics to figures such as Mo Farah and Dame Kelly Holmes.

questions.question: Bobby Moore captained the English team that won which tournament in 1966?
questions.explanation:
Bobby Moore captained England's football team to the 1966 World Cup, England's only international football tournament victory.

The Ashes is a cricket series between England and Australia — relevant to cricket, not football.

questions.question: Sir Ian Botham captained the English team and holds records in which sport?
questions.explanation:
Sir Ian Botham captained the English cricket team and holds records for both batting and bowling.

Football relates to Bobby Moore, rugby to the Six Nations, and tennis to Andy Murray and Wimbledon.

questions.question: Jayne Torvill and Christopher Dean won Olympic gold in 1984 for which discipline?
questions.explanation:
Torvill and Dean won gold for ice dancing in 1984 and in four consecutive world championships.

Rowing relates to Redgrave, cycling to Hoy and Wiggins, and swimming to Paralympian Ellie Simmonds.

questions.question: Baroness Tanni Grey-Thompson won 16 Paralympic medals in what kind of racing?
questions.explanation:
Baroness Tanni Grey-Thompson, a wheelchair athlete, won 16 Paralympic medals (11 gold) and the London Marathon six times.

Sailing relates to Dame Ellen MacArthur, and cycling to Sir Chris Hoy.

questions.question: Dame Kelly Holmes won two Olympic gold medals in 2004 in which sport?
questions.explanation:
Dame Kelly Holmes won two golds for running at the 2004 Olympics.

Cycling relates to Chris Hoy, swimming to Ellie Simmonds, and rowing to Steve Redgrave.

questions.question: In 2004, Dame Ellen MacArthur became the fastest person to do what?
questions.explanation:
Dame Ellen MacArthur became the fastest person to sail around the world single-handed in 2004.

Sir Francis Chichester was the first to do so, in 1966/67 — relevant to that earlier achievement.

questions.question: Sir Chris Hoy is a Scottish Olympic champion in which sport?
questions.explanation:
Sir Chris Hoy is a Scottish cyclist who won six gold and one silver Olympic medals.

Rowing relates to Redgrave, athletics to Mo Farah, and sailing to Ellen MacArthur.

questions.question: Jessica Ennis won the 2012 Olympic gold medal in which event?
questions.explanation:
Jessica Ennis won the 2012 heptathlon, which includes seven track and field events.

The other events are individual disciplines, not the multi-event competition she won.

questions.question: Andy Murray, a Scottish tennis player, won which title in 2012?
questions.explanation:
Andy Murray won the 2012 US Open, the first British man to win a Grand Slam singles title since 1936.

In the same year he won Olympic gold and was runner-up at Wimbledon, so Wimbledon relates to a different result.

questions.question: Ellie Simmonds won Paralympic gold medals in which sport at the 2008 and 2012 Games?
questions.explanation:
Ellie Simmonds won gold medals for swimming and was the youngest member of the British team at the 2008 Games.

Wheelchair racing relates to Tanni Grey-Thompson and David Weir.

questions.question: The Grand National horse race is held at which course?
questions.explanation:
The Grand National is held at Aintree near Liverpool.

Royal Ascot is a Berkshire meeting attended by the Royal Family.

Ayr hosts the Scottish Grand National.

Newmarket has the National Horseracing Museum.

questions.question: The only golf 'Major' tournament held outside the United States is which?
questions.explanation:
The Open Championship is the only golf Major held outside the US, hosted by a different course each year.

The Ashes is cricket, the Six Nations is rugby, and the Grand National is horse racing.

questions.question: How tall is the London Eye?
questions.explanation:
The London Eye is a Ferris wheel 443 feet (135 metres) tall, on the southern bank of the Thames, built for the millennium.

The other heights are distractors and do not match the handbook.

questions.question: Loch Lomond is the largest expanse of what in mainland Britain?
questions.explanation:
Loch Lomond, in the Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park, is the largest expanse of fresh water in mainland Britain.

The other options do not describe what makes Loch Lomond notable.

questions.question: What is England's largest national park?
questions.explanation:
The Lake District is England's largest national park, famous for its lakes and mountains; its biggest stretch of water is Windermere.

Snowdonia is in Wales and Loch Lomond in Scotland.

questions.question: In 2007, television viewers voted which lake Britain's favourite view?
questions.explanation:
Wastwater, in the Lake District, was voted Britain's favourite view in 2007.

Windermere is the biggest stretch of water in the Lake District, and Loch Lomond is in Scotland — relevant to those places, not this poll.

questions.question: Roughly how long ago was the Giant's Causeway formed?
questions.explanation:
The Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland, a formation of volcanic lava columns, was formed about 50 million years ago.

The other timescales relate to human prehistory (e.g. first farmers ~6,000 years ago), not the Causeway's geology.

questions.question: Which of these is a criminal offence in the UK?
options: Selling drugs such as heroin or cocaine
questions.answer: Selling drugs such as heroin or cocaine
questions.explanation:
Selling or buying illegal drugs is a criminal offence.

Disputes over rent (housing law), faulty goods (consumer rights) and unfair dismissal (employment law) are civil matters, not criminal.

questions.question: Causing harassment, alarm or distress to someone because of their religion or ethnic origin is what?
options: A matter for the small claims court
questions.explanation:
Racial crime — causing harassment, alarm or distress because of religion or ethnic origin — is a criminal offence.

It is not a civil dispute, and the small claims court deals with minor civil money claims, not criminal matters.

questions.question: At what age is it legal to be sold tobacco products in the UK?
questions.explanation: It is illegal to sell tobacco products to anyone under 18. 16 is relevant to riding a moped or drinking with a meal in specific circumstances; 17 is the minimum age to drive a car.

questions.question: Which of these is dealt with under civil law rather than criminal law?
options: A dispute between a landlord and tenant
questions.answer: A dispute between a landlord and tenant
questions.explanation:
Landlord–tenant disputes (housing law) are civil matters.

Carrying a weapon, selling illegal drugs and racial harassment are all criminal offences, handled by the criminal courts.

questions.question: What is one of the main duties of the police in the UK?
questions.explanation:
The police protect life and property, prevent disturbances (keeping the peace), and prevent and detect crime.

Collecting taxes is done by HMRC, making laws is Parliament's role, and the courts are run by the judiciary.

questions.question: Police forces are headed by whom and are independent of what?
options: Chief Constables; independent of the government
The Home Secretary; independent of Parliament
questions.answer: Chief Constables; independent of the government
questions.explanation:
Police forces are headed by Chief Constables and are independent of the government.

Since 2012, elected Police and Crime Commissioners appoint the Chief Constable in England and Wales.

The other pairings are inaccurate.

questions.question: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, cases involving accused people aged 10 to 17 are normally heard where?
questions.explanation:
Cases involving those aged 10 to 17 are normally heard in a Youth Court.

The Crown Court hears the most serious cases.

County Courts deal with civil matters.

In Scotland the Children's Hearings System is used instead.

questions.question: In Scotland, which system deals with children and young people who have committed an offence?
questions.explanation:
Scotland uses the Children's Hearings System for children and young people.

Youth Courts, Magistrates' Courts and Crown Courts operate in England, Wales and Northern Ireland — so those are relevant to those parts of the UK.

questions.question: Which trained lawyers give legal advice and can represent clients in court?
questions.explanation:
Solicitors are trained lawyers who advise clients and represent them in court.

Magistrates decide cases in Magistrates' Courts.

Peers sit in the House of Lords.

Councillors serve on local authorities.

questions.question: In which year was the UK one of the first countries to sign the European Convention on Human Rights?
questions.explanation:
The UK signed the European Convention on Human Rights in 1950.

The Human Rights Act 1998 later incorporated it into UK law — so 1998 is relevant to that Act. 1689 and 1215 relate to the Bill of Rights and Magna Carta.

questions.question: Which of these is a right protected by the European Convention on Human Rights?
options: The right to a fair trial
The right to a government job
The right to avoid all taxes
questions.answer: The right to a fair trial
questions.explanation:
Convention rights include the right to life, prohibition of torture, prohibition of slavery and forced labour, liberty and security, a fair trial, freedom of thought and religion, and freedom of expression.

The other options are not Convention rights.

questions.question: Domestic violence in the UK is treated as what?
questions.explanation:
Domestic violence is a serious crime; anyone violent towards a partner can be prosecuted, and forcing a partner to have sex, including within marriage, can be charged as rape.

It is never a private-only or acceptable matter.

questions.question: Money raised from National Insurance Contributions helps pay for what?
options: State benefits, the state pension and the NHS
questions.answer: State benefits, the state pension and the NHS
questions.explanation:
National Insurance funds state benefits, the state retirement pension and the NHS.

General income tax pays for services such as roads, education, police and the armed forces — so those relate to income tax rather than National Insurance.

questions.question: Self-employed people pay their tax through which system?
questions.explanation:
Self-employed people pay tax through self-assessment, completing a tax return.

PAYE is used for employees, whose tax is deducted by their employer.

Council tax funds local services and is a separate charge.

questions.question: What is the minimum age to ride a moped in the UK?
questions.explanation: You must be at least 16 to ride a moped. 17 is the minimum age to drive a car or motorcycle. 18 relates to voting and buying alcohol.

questions.question: A UK driving licence is valid until the holder is what age, after which it is renewed every three years?
questions.explanation:
Drivers can use their licence until they are 70, after which it must be renewed every three years.

The other ages are distractors and do not match the handbook.

questions.question: The EEC was set up by which treaty, signed in 1957?
questions.explanation:
The EEC was set up by the Treaty of Rome, signed on 25 March 1957.

The Treaty (Act) of Union relates to England and Scotland (1707).

The Good Friday Agreement (1998) relates to Northern Ireland.

The other option is invented.

questions.question: How many countries originally founded the EEC in 1957?
questions.explanation:
Six western European countries founded the EEC: Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.

'27' is the current number of EU members, and '47' relates to the Council of Europe — so those are relevant to other bodies.

questions.question: According to the handbook, how many member countries does the Council of Europe have?
questions.explanation:
The handbook states the Council of Europe has 47 member countries and is responsible for human rights, with no power to make laws.

'27' relates to the EU, '54' to the Commonwealth, and '15' to the total members of the UN Security Council.

questions.question: How many members sit on the UN Security Council?
questions.explanation:
There are 15 members on the UN Security Council.

The UK is one of the five permanent members — so '5' is relevant to the permanent members, not the total.

'27' and '47' relate to the EU and Council of Europe.

questions.question: Membership of the Commonwealth is described how?
questions.explanation:
Commonwealth membership is voluntary, and the Commonwealth can suspend members but has no power over them.

Its core values are democracy, good government and the rule of law.

The other options misdescribe how membership works.

questions.question: According to the handbook's population table, what was the UK population in 1901?
questions.explanation: The population in 1901 was 40 million. 20 million relates to 1851, 50 million to 1951, and 8 million to 1801 — so those figures are relevant to those earlier years.

questions.question: What has mainly driven faster UK population growth in recent years?
questions.explanation:
Migration into the UK and longer life expectancy have driven recent population growth.

Emigration reduces population, and the Industrial Revolution relates to a much earlier historical period.

questions.question: Roughly what proportion of the UK population has a parent or grandparent born outside the UK?
questions.explanation:
Post-war immigration means nearly 10% of the population has a parent or grandparent born outside the UK.

The other proportions are distractors and do not match the handbook.

questions.question: Which statement about Scottish and Northern Irish banknotes is correct?
options: They are valid everywhere in the UK, but shops do not have to accept them
They are only valid in Scotland and Northern Ireland
They are not legal at all
They must be exchanged before use in England
questions.answer: They are valid everywhere in the UK, but shops do not have to accept them
questions.explanation:
Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own banknotes, valid everywhere in the UK, though shops and businesses are not obliged to accept them.

The other statements are inaccurate.

questions.question: In which year did Queen Elizabeth II's reign begin?
questions.explanation: Queen Elizabeth II's reign began in 1952, on her father's death; she died in 2022. 2012 was her Diamond Jubilee (60 years). 2022 is the year she died and King Charles III became sovereign.

questions.question: Who is the heir apparent to King Charles III?
questions.explanation:
William, Prince of Wales, is the heir apparent.

His children (Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis) are next in line after him.

Prince Edward is a separate member of the Royal Family.

questions.question: New citizens swear or affirm allegiance to whom at the citizenship ceremony?
options: His Majesty King Charles the Third, his Heirs and Successors
questions.answer: His Majesty King Charles the Third, his Heirs and Successors
questions.explanation:
The oath and affirmation of allegiance are made to His Majesty King Charles the Third, his Heirs and Successors, according to law.

Allegiance is not sworn to the Prime Minister, Parliament or the Archbishop.

questions.question: Since 1999, hereditary peers have lost which right?
options: The automatic right to attend the House of Lords
The right to vote in general elections
The right to stand as an MP
questions.answer: The automatic right to attend the House of Lords
questions.explanation:
Since 1999, hereditary peers have lost the automatic right to attend the House of Lords and now elect a few of their number to represent them.

The other rights are unaffected by this change.

questions.question: What is a by-election?
options: An election held when an MP dies or resigns
A general election held every five years
An election for the House of Lords
A vote to change the monarch
questions.answer: An election held when an MP dies or resigns
questions.explanation:
A by-election is held in a constituency when its MP dies or resigns.

A general election is the nationwide election held at least every five years.

Peers are not elected by the public, and the monarch is not chosen by a vote.

questions.question: How many members does the Welsh Parliament/Assembly have?
questions.explanation: The Welsh body has 60 members (AMs), based in Cardiff. 129 relates to the Scottish Parliament (MSPs), 90 to the Northern Ireland Assembly (MLAs), and 650 to MPs in the UK House of Commons.

questions.question: How many members does the Northern Ireland Assembly have?
questions.explanation: The Northern Ireland Assembly has 90 members (MLAs), based at Stormont, elected by proportional representation with a power-sharing arrangement. 60 relates to Wales and 129 to Scotland.

questions.question: In which year was the original Northern Ireland Parliament established?
questions.explanation: A Northern Ireland Parliament was established in 1922 when Ireland was divided; it was abolished in 1972. 1998 relates to the Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement and 2007 to the Assembly running successfully again.

questions.question: The official reports of proceedings in Parliament are published in what?
questions.explanation:
Parliamentary proceedings are published in Hansard.

The Domesday Book was a Norman-era land survey.

The Beveridge Report set out the welfare state.

The Yellow Pages was a business phone directory.

questions.question: Which cabinet minister is responsible for crime, policing and immigration?
questions.explanation:
The Home Secretary is responsible for crime, policing and immigration.

The Chancellor of the Exchequer handles the economy.

The Foreign Secretary manages relations with other countries.

The Speaker chairs Commons debates.

questions.question: Who can vote in all UK public elections, including general elections?
options: UK, Commonwealth and Irish Republic citizens resident in the UK
Only people born in the UK
questions.answer: UK, Commonwealth and Irish Republic citizens resident in the UK
questions.explanation:
Adult citizens of the UK, the Commonwealth and the Irish Republic who are resident in the UK can vote in all public elections.

The voting age is 18, not 16, and citizenship is broader than being UK-born or a passport holder.

questions.question: To vote in an election, your name must be on what?
questions.explanation:
You must have your name on the electoral register to vote.

Hansard records parliamentary debates, the Domesday Book was a Norman survey, and the Yellow Pages was a phone directory — none of which register voters.

questions.question: On election day, what hours are polling stations open?
questions.explanation:
Polling stations are open from 7.00 am until 10.00 pm on election day.

The other times are distractors and do not match the handbook.

questions.question: Which of these groups cannot stand for public office?
options: Members of the armed forces and civil servants
questions.answer: Members of the armed forces and civil servants
questions.explanation:
Exceptions to standing for office include members of the armed forces, civil servants and people found guilty of certain criminal offences.

Being retired, over 65, or a Commonwealth citizen does not by itself prevent someone from standing.

questions.question: In which year did the process of devolving powers to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland begin?
questions.explanation: Since 1997, some powers have been devolved to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, with the Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly first meeting in 1999. 1928 relates to full voting equality, 1969 to the voting age of 18, and 2010 to the coalition government.

questions.question: Pressure and lobby groups try to do what?
questions.explanation:
Pressure and lobby groups (such as the CBI, Greenpeace and Liberty) try to influence government policy.

They do not elect the monarch, run the courts, or collect taxes.

questions.question: The CBI (Confederation of British Industry) represents whose views?
questions.explanation:
The CBI represents the views of British business.

Greenpeace campaigns on the environment, and Liberty on human rights — so those causes relate to other pressure groups.

questions.question: The shadow cabinet's role is to do what?
options: Challenge the government and put forward alternative policies
questions.answer: Challenge the government and put forward alternative policies
questions.explanation:
The shadow cabinet, appointed by the leader of the opposition, challenges the government and offers alternative policies.

Chairing Commons debates is the Speaker's role, and local councils are run separately.

questions.question: Local authorities (councils) are funded by what?
options: Central government money and local taxes
questions.answer: Central government money and local taxes
questions.explanation:
Local authorities are funded by money from central government and by local taxes.

They are not funded by the monarch, the EU, or the Church of England.

questions.question: Life peers are appointed by the monarch on whose advice?
questions.explanation:
Life peers are appointed by the monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister, and may include people nominated by other party leaders or an independent Appointments Commission.

The other roles do not advise on peerages.

questions.question: Which of these is listed as a shared responsibility of everyone in the UK?
options: To vote in local and national elections
To belong to a political party
questions.answer: To vote in local and national elections
questions.explanation:
Shared responsibilities include obeying the law, respecting others' rights, looking after your family and the environment, and voting in elections.

Weekly church attendance, military service and party membership are not required.

questions.question: What are the three key roles of school governors?
options: Setting strategic direction, ensuring accountability, and monitoring performance
Teaching lessons, marking work, and setting exams
Running the canteen, cleaning, and transport
Appointing the police, judges, and MPs
questions.answer: Setting strategic direction, ensuring accountability, and monitoring performance
questions.explanation:
School governors set the strategic direction of the school, ensure accountability, and monitor and evaluate school performance.

Teaching and day-to-day tasks are done by staff, not governors.

questions.question: Roughly how long does giving blood take?
questions.explanation:
Giving blood takes about an hour.

Donated blood is used by hospitals to help people with a wide range of injuries and illnesses.

The other durations do not match the handbook.

questions.question: You can volunteer with the police as which of these?
options: A Police and Crime Commissioner appointee
questions.explanation:
You can volunteer with the police as a special constable or a lay representative.

A Chief Constable heads a police force (a senior paid role).

You can separately apply to become a magistrate, but that is a court role, not a police one.

questions.question: The NSPCC is a charity that works mainly with whom?
questions.explanation:
The NSPCC (National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children) works with children.

Age UK works with older people, the PDSA with animals, and Crisis and Shelter with the homeless — so those causes relate to other charities.

questions.question: Which charity works with older people?
questions.explanation:
Age UK works with older people.

The NSPCC works with children, the PDSA with animals, and Friends of the Earth on the environment.

questions.question: Which of these is a benefit of volunteering mentioned in the handbook?
options: Meeting new people and practising English or work skills
questions.answer: Meeting new people and practising English or work skills
questions.explanation:
Volunteering can help you meet new people, practise English, develop work skills and improve your CV.

Volunteering is unpaid work for good causes, so payment, tax exemption and free licences are not benefits of it.

questions.question: The Concorde supersonic aircraft was retired from service in which year?
questions.explanation:
Concorde was retired in 2003.

It first flew in 1969 and began carrying passengers in 1976 — so those years relate to its introduction, not its retirement. 1990 relates to the first World Wide Web transfer.

questions.question: In the early 1970s, Britain admitted around 28,000 people of Indian origin forced to leave which country?
questions.explanation:
Britain admitted around 28,000 people of Indian origin forced to leave Uganda in the early 1970s.

India and Pakistan were sources of earlier recruited workers, and Kenya is a distractor here.

questions.question: Which Welsh author, whose parents were Norwegian, wrote 'Charlie and the Chocolate Factory'?
questions.explanation:
Roald Dahl, born in Wales to Norwegian parents, wrote Charlie and the Chocolate Factory and George's Marvellous Medicine.

Dylan Thomas was a Welsh poet.

J K Rowling wrote Harry Potter, and Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings.

questions.question: Which prize for the best UK and Ireland album is awarded each September?
questions.explanation:
The Mercury Music Prize is awarded each September for the best album from the UK and Ireland.

The Turner Prize is for contemporary art, the Man Booker Prize for fiction, and the Laurence Olivier Awards for theatre.

questions.question: The National Eisteddfod is an annual cultural festival held in which nation, largely in its own language?
questions.explanation:
The National Eisteddfod of Wales is a cultural festival of music, dance, art and performance, largely in Welsh, with important poetry competitions.

It is specific to Wales.

questions.question: Which British silent-film star was famous for his 'tramp' character?
questions.explanation:
Sir Charlie Chaplin became famous in silent movies for his tramp character.

Sir Alfred Hitchcock, Sir David Lean and Ridley Scott were directors rather than silent-film comedy actors.

questions.question: Which day, on 1 April, is when people play jokes on each other until midday?
questions.explanation:
April Fool's Day (1 April) is when people play jokes until midday.

Valentine's Day is 14 February, Halloween is 31 October, and Hogmanay is the Scottish name for New Year's Eve (31 December).

questions.question: In Scotland, what is New Year's Eve (31 December) called?
questions.explanation:
In Scotland, 31 December is called Hogmanay, and for some Scots it is a bigger celebration than Christmas.

Boxing Day is 26 December, Shrove Tuesday precedes Lent, and Vaisakhi is a Sikh festival.

questions.question: Which two long-running soap operas are named in the handbook?
questions.explanation:
Coronation Street and EastEnders are the soap operas named as popular programmes.

The other titles are real British shows but are not the ones cited in the handbook here.

questions.question: What penalty can you face for watching TV without a TV licence?
questions.explanation:
You can be fined up to £1,000 for watching TV without a licence.

People over 75 can apply for a free licence and blind people get a 50% discount.

The other penalties are not the consequence described.

questions.question: In the 2009 Citizenship Survey, what percentage of people said they had no religion?
questions.explanation:
About 21% said they had no religion. 70% identified as Christian, and 4% as Muslim — so those figures relate to those groups.

The UK guarantees everyone the right to choose their religion or none.

questions.question: The Moderator is the chairperson of the General Assembly of which church?
questions.explanation:
The Moderator chairs the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland and is appointed for one year.

The Church of England is led spiritually by the Archbishop of Canterbury, with the monarch as its head.

questions.question: Which day is St David's Day, the patron saint's day of Wales?
questions.explanation: St David's Day (Wales) is 1 March. 17 March is St Patrick's Day (Northern Ireland), 23 April is St George's Day (England), and 30 November is St Andrew's Day (Scotland).

questions.question: Which day is St Andrew's Day, the patron saint's day of Scotland?
questions.explanation: St Andrew's Day (Scotland) is 30 November. 1 March is St David's Day (Wales), 17 March is St Patrick's Day (Northern Ireland), and 23 April is St George's Day (England).

questions.question: The Rest of Ireland (outside Northern Ireland) is what?
questions.explanation:
The rest of Ireland is an independent country (the Republic of Ireland).

Crown dependencies are the Channel Islands and Isle of Man; British overseas territories include St Helena and the Falklands; Great Britain is England, Scotland and Wales.

questions.question: In which cathedral is there famous medieval stained glass telling Bible stories?
questions.explanation:
York Minster is famous for its medieval stained glass.

St Paul's Cathedral was rebuilt by Christopher Wren after the Great Fire.

Westminster Abbey is where several composers and poets are associated.

The Banqueting House is not a cathedral.

questions.question: In 1776, how many American colonies declared their independence?
questions.explanation:
In 1776, 13 American colonies declared independence, which Britain recognised in 1783.

'9' relates to the number of countries granted independence in 1947, and '6' to the founding members of the EEC — so those numbers relate to other topics.

questions.question: In which year did the UK officially become a member of the EEC?
questions.explanation: The UK joined the EEC in 1973. 1957 is when the EEC was founded. 2016 is the year of the EU membership referendum (Brexit vote), and 1993 is a distractor here.

questions.question: Which team of scientists, led by Ernest Rutherford, first 'split the atom'?
options: Scientists working at Manchester and Cambridge universities
A team in the United States only
questions.answer: Scientists working at Manchester and Cambridge universities
questions.explanation:
Scientists led by Ernest Rutherford, working at Manchester and then Cambridge University, were the first to 'split the atom' and took part in the Manhattan Project.

The other locations are inaccurate.

questions.question: Which of these is one of the fundamental principles of British life?
options: Loyalty to a single political party
questions.explanation:
The fundamental principles are democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance of different faiths and beliefs, and participation in community life.

A state-controlled press contradicts the UK's free press, and the other options are not British values.

questions.question: Which Scottish painter is best known for portraits and the work 'The Origin of Painting'?
questions.explanation:
David Allan was a Scottish portrait painter known for 'The Origin of Painting'.

Joseph Turner was a landscape painter, John Constable painted Dedham Vale, and Henry Moore was a sculptor.

questions.question: Which artist is considered to have raised the profile of landscape painting, and gives his name to a major art prize?
questions.explanation:
Joseph Turner was an influential landscape painter, and the Turner Prize is named after him.

Gainsborough was a portrait painter, Lucian Freud is known for portraits, and David Hockney for pop art.

questions.question: The Pre-Raphaelites were a group of artists active in which period?
options: The second half of the 19th century
questions.answer: The second half of the 19th century
questions.explanation:
The Pre-Raphaelites (including Holman Hunt, Dante Gabriel Rossetti and Sir John Millais) painted detailed pictures on religious or literary themes in the second half of the 19th century.

The 1960s relates to pop art (David Hockney).

questions.question: Sir John Lavery was a successful portrait painter from which part of the UK?
questions.explanation:
Sir John Lavery was a Northern Irish portrait painter whose work included painting the Royal Family.

John Petts was a Welsh artist, and David Allan a Scottish painter — so those nations relate to other artists.

questions.question: John Petts was a Welsh artist best known for what?
questions.explanation:
John Petts, a Welsh artist, is best known for engravings and stained glass.

Bronze sculptures relate to Henry Moore, and pop art to David Hockney.

questions.question: Lucian Freud, a German-born British artist, is best known for what?
questions.explanation:
Lucian Freud is best known for his portraits.

Stained glass relates to John Petts, landscapes to Turner and Constable, and abstract sculpture to Henry Moore.

questions.question: David Hockney was an important contributor to which 1960s art movement?
questions.explanation:
David Hockney contributed to the 'pop art' movement of the 1960s.

The Pre-Raphaelites were a 19th-century group.

Impressionism and Cubism are movements not attributed to Hockney in the handbook.

questions.question: Which of these is a modern British architect who has worked on major projects worldwide?
questions.explanation:
Modern British architects include Sir Norman Foster, Lord (Richard) Rogers and Dame Zaha Hadid.

Sir Christopher Wren, Inigo Jones and Robert Adam were architects of earlier centuries.

questions.question: Which garden designer often worked with the architect Edwin Lutyens on colourful gardens?
questions.explanation:
Gertrude Jekyll designed colourful gardens, often working with Edwin Lutyens.

'Capability' Brown designed natural-looking landscapes in an earlier era.

Clarice Cliff and Mary Quant were designers in ceramics and fashion.

questions.question: Which annual event showcases garden design from Britain and around the world?
questions.explanation:
The annual Chelsea Flower Show showcases garden design.

The Edinburgh Fringe features theatre and comedy, the Proms is classical music, and the Turner Prize is for contemporary art.

questions.question: Thomas Chippendale was an 18th-century British designer of what?
questions.explanation:
Thomas Chippendale designed furniture in the 18th century.

Clarice Cliff designed Art Deco ceramics, and figures like Mary Quant designed fashion — so those relate to other designers.

questions.question: Which of these is a leading British fashion designer of recent years?
questions.explanation:
Leading recent fashion designers include Mary Quant, Alexander McQueen and Vivienne Westwood.

Thomas Chippendale designed furniture, Clarice Cliff designed ceramics, and Sir Terence Conran was an interior designer.

questions.question: Which British writers have won the Nobel Prize in Literature?
options: William Golding, Seamus Heaney and Harold Pinter
J K Rowling and J R R Tolkien
questions.answer: William Golding, Seamus Heaney and Harold Pinter
questions.explanation:
The novelist Sir William Golding, poet Seamus Heaney and playwright Harold Pinter won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

Agatha Christie, Ian Fleming, Dickens, Austen, Rowling and Tolkien are famous but did not win it.

questions.question: The Man Booker Prize, awarded since 1968, is given for what?
questions.explanation:
The Man Booker Prize is awarded annually for the best fiction novel.

The Mercury Music Prize is for albums, the Turner Prize for contemporary art, and the Laurence Olivier Awards for theatre.

questions.question: Which author wrote Treasure Island and Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde?
questions.explanation:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote Treasure Island, Kidnapped and Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.

Thomas Hardy wrote Far from the Madding Crowd, Evelyn Waugh wrote Brideshead Revisited, and Graham Greene wrote Brighton Rock.

questions.question: Which author's best-known novels focus on rural society, including Far from the Madding Crowd?
questions.explanation:
Thomas Hardy wrote about rural society in works such as Far from the Madding Crowd and Jude the Obscure.

Dickens wrote about urban life, Austen about marriage and family, and Kingsley Amis wrote Lucky Jim.

questions.question: Which novel is Evelyn Waugh perhaps best known for?
questions.explanation:
Evelyn Waugh is best known for Brideshead Revisited.

Lucky Jim was written by Sir Kingsley Amis, Brighton Rock by Graham Greene, and Great Expectations by Charles Dickens.

questions.question: Which Anglo-Saxon poem tells of its hero's battles against monsters?
options: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
questions.explanation:
Beowulf is an Anglo-Saxon poem about a hero's battles against monsters.

The Canterbury Tales and Sir Gawain and the Green Knight are from the Middle Ages, and Paradise Lost is by John Milton.

questions.question: The medieval poem 'Sir Gawain and the Green Knight' concerns a knight at whose court?
questions.explanation:
Sir Gawain and the Green Knight concerns a knight at the court of King Arthur.

The other kings are real historical or legendary figures but are not linked to this poem in the handbook.

questions.question: Which poet wrote 'The Daffodils' ('I wander'd lonely as a cloud')?
questions.explanation:
William Wordsworth wrote 'The Daffodils', inspired by nature.

William Blake wrote 'The Tyger', Lord Byron wrote 'She Walks in Beauty', and Wilfred Owen wrote about the First World War.

questions.question: The poem beginning 'Tyger! Tyger! Burning bright' was written by whom?
questions.explanation:
William Blake wrote 'The Tyger'.

Wordsworth wrote 'The Daffodils', Byron wrote 'She Walks in Beauty', and Robert Browning wrote 'Home Thoughts from Abroad'.

questions.question: Wilfred Owen and Siegfried Sassoon are especially known for writing about what?
options: Their experiences in the First World War
questions.answer: Their experiences in the First World War
questions.explanation:
Wilfred Owen (who wrote 'Anthem for Doomed Youth') and Siegfried Sassoon wrote about their First World War experiences.

The Scottish landscape relates to Sir Walter Scott, and nature to Wordsworth.

questions.question: Where are many famous British poets buried or commemorated?
questions.explanation:
Many poets are buried or commemorated in Poets' Corner in Westminster Abbey.

The Tower of London holds the Crown Jewels, Tate Modern is an art gallery, and the Globe is a theatre linked to Shakespeare.

questions.question: Who wrote the music for shows including Cats and The Phantom of the Opera?
questions.explanation:
Andrew Lloyd Webber wrote Cats, The Phantom of the Opera and (with Tim Rice) Jesus Christ Superstar and Evita.

Gilbert and Sullivan wrote 19th-century comic operas, and Britten and Elgar were classical composers.

questions.question: In a traditional British pantomime, the 'Dame' is what?
options: A woman character played by a man
questions.answer: A woman character played by a man
questions.explanation:
The Dame is a traditional pantomime character, a woman played by a man.

Pantomimes also often feature a pantomime horse or cow played by two actors, but the Dame specifically refers to the man-played woman.

questions.question: The Brit Awards are given in which field?
questions.explanation:
The Brit Awards are annual music awards (e.g. best British group and solo artist).

Film awards are the BAFTAs, theatre awards the Laurence Olivier Awards, and literature the Man Booker Prize.

questions.question: Which of these is a well-known British music festival?
questions.explanation:
Famous music festivals include Glastonbury, the Isle of Wight Festival and the V Festival.

The Chelsea Flower Show is about gardens, Royal Ascot is horse racing, and the Edinburgh Fringe is theatre and comedy.

questions.question: Who was the first person to sail single-handed around the world, in 1966/67?
questions.explanation:
Sir Francis Chichester was the first to sail single-handed around the world (1966/67).

Sir Robin Knox-Johnston was first to do so non-stop.

Dame Ellen MacArthur later became the fastest to do it single-handed.

questions.question: Sir Robin Knox-Johnston was the first person to sail around the world single-handed in what way?
options: Using only sails made in Britain
questions.explanation:
Sir Robin Knox-Johnston was the first to sail around the world single-handed without stopping.

Being the first single-handed relates to Sir Francis Chichester, and the fastest to Dame Ellen MacArthur.

questions.question: The most famous UK sailing event is held where?
options: Cowes, on the Isle of Wight
questions.answer: Cowes, on the Isle of Wight
questions.explanation:
The most famous sailing event is held at Cowes on the Isle of Wight.

Aintree hosts the Grand National (horse racing), St Andrews is the home of golf, and Wimbledon hosts tennis.

questions.question: There is a popular yearly rowing race on the Thames between which two universities?
questions.explanation:
The annual Boat Race on the Thames is rowed between Oxford and Cambridge Universities.

The other pairings are distractors and do not match the handbook.

questions.question: Which of these is a recent British Formula 1 World Champion?
questions.explanation:
Recent British Formula 1 World Champions include Damon Hill, Lewis Hamilton and Jenson Button.

Andy Murray is a tennis player, and Chris Hoy and Bradley Wiggins are cyclists.

questions.question: In which year did motor-car racing start in the UK?
questions.explanation: Motor-car racing in the UK started in 1902. 1966 relates to England winning the football World Cup, and 1948 to the UK hosting the Olympics — so those years relate to other sporting facts.

questions.question: How many ski centres are there in Scotland, according to the handbook?
questions.explanation:
There are five ski centres in Scotland, as well as Europe's longest dry ski slope near Edinburgh.

'15' is relevant to the number of national parks in England, Wales and Scotland.

questions.question: David Weir is a Paralympian who competes in what?
questions.explanation:
David Weir is a wheelchair-racing Paralympian who won six gold medals over two Games and the London Marathon six times.

Swimming relates to Ellie Simmonds, and sailing to Ellen MacArthur.

questions.question: The National Trust is helped to run by roughly how many volunteers?
questions.explanation:
The National Trust, founded in 1895 by three volunteers, now has more than 61,000 volunteers.

The other figures are distractors and do not match the handbook.

questions.question: Which of these is a UK coin denomination?
questions.explanation:
UK coins are 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2. £5 and £20 are banknotes, not coins — so those relate to notes.

There is no £100 note in general circulation.

questions.question: Which of these is a UK banknote denomination?
questions.explanation:
UK notes are £5, £10, £20 and £50. £1 and £2 are coins — so those relate to coins.

There is no standard £100 note.

questions.question: How often does the cabinet usually meet?
questions.explanation:
The cabinet usually meets weekly to make important decisions about government policy.

'Every five years' relates to how often general elections must be held at the latest, not cabinet meetings.

questions.question: Which cabinet minister is responsible for relations with foreign countries?
questions.explanation:
The Foreign Secretary manages relationships with foreign countries.

The Home Secretary handles crime, policing and immigration, and the Chancellor handles the economy.

The Speaker chairs Commons debates.

questions.question: Florence Nightingale established a training school for nurses at which London hospital?
questions.explanation:
Florence Nightingale established the Nightingale Training School for nurses at St Thomas' Hospital in London.

Stoke Mandeville is relevant to the origins of the Paralympic Games.

questions.question: When do UK bank holidays (other than religious ones) generally fall?
options: Early May, late May or early June, and August
questions.answer: Early May, late May or early June, and August
questions.explanation:
Bank holidays with no religious significance fall at the beginning of May, in late May or early June, and in August (with an extra one in Northern Ireland in July).

They are not weekly or restricted to December.

questions.question: The Millennium Stadium, a major UK sporting venue, is in which city?
questions.explanation:
The Millennium Stadium is in Cardiff.

Wembley Stadium is in London.

Glasgow has the SECC as a music venue, and Manchester is a distractor here.

questions.question: Which composer was strongly influenced by traditional English folk music?
questions.explanation:
Ralph Vaughan Williams was strongly influenced by traditional English folk music.

Handel wrote Messiah, Purcell was an organist at Westminster Abbey, and Britten wrote operas such as Peter Grimes.

questions.question: Sir William Walton wrote marches for the coronations of which monarchs?
options: King George VI and Queen Elizabeth II
King Charles II and James II
King Henry VIII and Edward VI
questions.answer: King George VI and Queen Elizabeth II
questions.explanation:
Sir William Walton wrote coronation marches for King George VI and Queen Elizabeth II, and is also known for Façade and Belshazzar's Feast.

The other monarchs are from earlier eras.

questions.question: Which poet, known as 'The Bard', wrote in the Scots language?
questions.explanation:
Robert Burns, 'The Bard', wrote in Scots, English with Scottish words, and standard English, and wrote 'Auld Lang Syne'.

Dylan Thomas was Welsh, and Wordsworth and Milton were English poets.

questions.question: Which Scottish physician was a co-discoverer of insulin, used to treat diabetes?
questions.explanation:
John MacLeod, a Scottish physician, was a co-discoverer of insulin.

Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, Alan Turing devised the Turing machine, and Francis Crick helped discover the structure of DNA.

questions.question: The structure of the DNA molecule was discovered in which year, through work at British universities?
questions.explanation: The structure of DNA was discovered in 1953; Francis Crick, one of those awarded the Nobel Prize, was British. 1928 relates to penicillin, 1990 to the first web transfer, and 1996 to Dolly the sheep.

questions.question: Sir Peter Mansfield was a co-inventor of which medical scanner?
questions.explanation:
Sir Peter Mansfield co-invented the MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scanner, which produces non-invasive images of internal organs.

The other technologies are not the one attributed to him in the handbook.

questions.question: The radio telescope built by Sir Bernard Lovell is located where?
questions.explanation:
Sir Bernard Lovell built the radio telescope at Jodrell Bank in Cheshire, for many years the biggest in the world.

Enfield relates to the first ATM, and Stratford to the 2012 Olympic site.
